 Opinion | National news outlets landed the biggest stories of the 2026 campaign. That’s a problem.
 Out-of-towners consistently beat local reporters, revealing the hollowing out of newsrooms in towns and cities across the country
 A campaign volunteer hangs a sign before Democratic Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner speaks at a town hall in Ogunquit, Maine, Wednesday, Oct. 22, 2025. (AP Photo/Caleb Jones) 
 By:
 Paul Farhi 
 November 12, 2026 
 -->
 -->
 The two most important stories about the Senate race in Maine this year arguably involved revelations of alleged sexual misconduct by the Democratic candidate, Graham Platner, and allegations of corruption by the Republican incumbent, Susan Collins. The first story brought down Platner’s candidacy; the second may have contributed to Collins’ defeat at the polls last week.
 The striking thing about both stories is that neither one was published by a news outlet based anywhere near Maine. The New York Times and Politico did in Platner. ProPublica and The Intercept dug up the allegations against Collins.
 This wasn’t a fluke or a one-off. Some of the biggest and most consequential investigative work on the 2026 election came from reporters employed by national news organizations, parachuting in, as it were, to scoop the locals in their own backyards.
 The revelation that Democrats in Alaska surreptitiously recruited a Senate candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to stack the ballot against the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan? That story was broken by a Times reporter, Kellen Browning, six days before Election Day. Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall’s aggressive pursuit of hundreds of former patients who owed him money for medical services? That was by another Times journalist, Sarah Kliff. Details about spousal and child abuse allegations involving Rep. Max Miller of Ohio? You didn’t see it first in Miller’s hometown paper; the story was a result of digging by a reporter at Mother Jones magazine, Abby Vesoulis. Another Mother Jones reporter, Noah Lanard, did the investigative pieces detailing Florida Rep. Cory Mills’ history of restraining orders, business issues and stolen-valor allegations.
 More than just counting scoops, the fact that out-of-towners consistently beat the local beat reporters suggests a serious underlying problem. For years, academics and others have been pointing to a growing crisis in local reporting — the hollowing out of newsrooms in towns and cities across the country. One consequence of this may have been on display during the 2026 election cycle, when the local news media was often the dog that didn’t, and perhaps couldn’t, hunt.
 Well-staffed regional newspapers — the Miami Herald, Chicago Tribune, Boston Globe, Baltimore Sun, among them — used to be the source of investigations, local and otherwise. The Globe’s Spotlight team broke the Catholic clergy abuse scandal in 2002; the Herald’s Julie K. Brown single-handedly revived the case against Jeffrey Epstein in 2018 with her series, “Perversion of Justice.” 
 A few regional outlets did step up during the campaign, landing big stories. The San Francisco Chronicle’s Alexei Koseff and Sophia Bollag ended the political career of California Rep. Eric Swalwell, the leading candidate for governor, by reporting on a former Swalwell staffer’s allegation of sexual assault. The San Antonio Express-News and The Texas Tribune dropped bombshells nearly simultaneously in February, disclosing Rep. Tony Gonzales’ relationship with a staffer who later committed suicide by lighting herself on fire. Swalwell and Gonzales resigned from Congress.
 But years of declining advertising and waning subscriptions have sapped the investigative muscle, as well as routine reporting, of local news organizations. A growing number of American counties have turned into news deserts, with no professional news reporting at all.
 The parlous financial state of local news weighs against the time and expense necessary for sustained reporting. A particularly aggressive bit of reporting or a devastating scoop can even backfire, eliciting charges of bias and demands to cancel subscriptions. Steve Greenlee, the former editor of the Portland Press Herald in Maine, told the Columbia Journalism Review last week that he would often hear from readers who were angry that the paper’s reporting didn’t match the opinions expressed on talk radio or Fox News. The fear, he said, is that subscriptions would drop so much “that you won’t have a newspaper anymore.”
 Hence the drift toward the “nationalization” of deep political reporting by outfits with both deeper pockets and few local ties. “The big players in D.C. and New York City are taking on an oversized role in investigative journalism with local ramifications,” said Michael Socolow, a journalism professor at the University of Maine. National news organizations are stepping in where diminished newspapers and local TV stations “don’t have the investment or protection anymore.”
 Socolow watched the Platner and Collins stories unfold in his home state. He noted its antecedents: The Bangor Daily News had the first whiff of Collins’ questionable relationship with a defense contractor in February 2022. The conservative Maine Wire, meanwhile, had inklings about Platner in May, including screenshots from dating apps that suggested problematic personal behavior.
 But the big picture behind both stories remained hidden until reporters from national outlets showed up. The Times’ Katie Glueck and Lisa Lerer reported in late May that Platner’s wife had warned campaign officials that Platner had been sending sexual messages to as many as a dozen women while married. A few days later, Glueck and Lerer reported on Platner’s troubling behavior with women, including a former girlfriend’s accounts of physical altercations. The final beat: Politico’s Jessica Piper and Adam Wren broke the most serious allegations , leading to Platner’s withdrawal from the race two days later (it surely helped that Piper is an alum of the Bangor Daily News and maintained her local connections).
 The failure, or mere inability, of local outlets to nail the larger story was reminiscent of the coverage of former Rep. George Santos’ campaign in 2022. A small newspaper, the North Shore Leader, reported oddities and anomalies in Santos’ biography before Election Day, and opined that he was “sketchy.” But the breadth of Santos’ fabrications didn’t emerge until the Times’ Grace Ashford and Michael Gold spent weeks looking into Santos’ claims. By then, however, Santos had already been elected.
 One of the obvious advantages of a national news organization is its reach and prestige; sources may be more willing to divulge sensitive information to an outlet with the mammoth impact of the Times than one that circulates in one town or region. But Big Media’s structural advantage over its local brethren goes beyond staff size, circulation and bankroll. National reporters don’t live in the communities they wade into, which immunizes them and their employers from social pressure, political retaliation and advertiser boycotts that could paralyze a smaller newsroom. Further, a news organization with a strong presence in Washington ensures sources and connections that don’t exist on the local level. Local news organizations used to have bureaus in Washington; these have been gutted, too.
 The good news is that reporters still dug up important stories during the campaign. As Socolow put it, “investigative journalism still matters in 2026.”
 But out-of-town journalism isn’t a substitute for the local kind. Scandals and corruption don’t just occur with every election cycle, and they don’t just happen in Washington. They’re down the street and across town. The big scoops by national reporters are, in some ways, evidence of failure, suggesting that the media system works at the top but is crumbling at the foundation.
 Rigorous and probing news reporting “takes money, time, credibility, relationships, and independence,” Socolow said. Unfortunately, “those are much more difficult to secure in local newsrooms today.”
 This kind of journalism doesn’t fund itself.
